nodes.label: OpenAI-compatible model client
nodes.summary: One thin chat client where the host is only base_url + key, so any open-weight provider swaps in.
nodes.whyItMatters: Provider lock-in is the first architecture decision; a single wire format keeps ablations across hosts honest.

nodes.label: One-shot baseline
nodes.summary: A single model call with ticket text and the named files; the floor every later agent must beat.
nodes.whyItMatters: Without a measured floor you cannot say the loop, context manager or judge added anything.

nodes.label: Tool schema design
nodes.summary: Typed, closed argument schemas per tool; the model sees only what it can use correctly.
nodes.whyItMatters: Tool descriptions and schemas are the agent-computer interface; most "model errors" are interface errors.

source.title: Writing effective tools for AI agents (Anthropic)

nodes.label: Tool allow-lists & unsafe tools
nodes.summary: Expose six tools; keep eval/run-code tools off even when the server offers them.
nodes.whyItMatters: An MCP server lists everything it can do; the allow-list is where least privilege starts.

nodes.label: Tool error taxonomy
nodes.summary: Closed set of tool error codes (stale-target, not-unique, not-found, not-allowed, failed) returned as observations.
nodes.whyItMatters: A model can only recover from an error it can tell apart; retries, metrics and dashboards all key off the code.

nodes.label: Accessibility-tree snapshots & refs
nodes.summary: The page is given to the model as an a11y tree whose elements carry refs; a stale ref is an error, not a guess.
nodes.whyItMatters: Snapshot-as-action-surface is cheaper than screenshots and gives stable targets, but blows the context window if uncapped.

nodes.label: Tool output truncation
nodes.summary: Cap every tool result at a byte budget before it reaches the model.
nodes.whyItMatters: Uncapped observations are the quickest way to burn a context window and a free-tier token quota.

source.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents (Anthropic)

nodes.label: Stop conditions & stop reasons
nodes.summary: Closed enum of why a run ended: submit, step-cap, token-cap, QuotaExceeded, stuck, timeouts, retry-cap.
nodes.whyItMatters: Every unbounded loop needs explicit exits, and a typed reason is what lets you count failure modes later.

nodes.label: Generate-run-revise loop
nodes.summary: Ask for a script, run it on buggy and fixed trees, revise until it reproduces or the cap hits.
nodes.whyItMatters: The smallest real agent loop: the environment, not the model, decides success.

nodes.label: Agent loop (tool-use)
nodes.summary: Model proposes a tool call, harness executes, result returns as an observation; repeat to a stop condition.
nodes.whyItMatters: The core primitive of every agent; frameworks differ in how they hide it, not in what it is.

nodes.label: Stuck detection
nodes.summary: Detect repeated actions, error loops or no-progress states, nudge once, then stop.
nodes.whyItMatters: Stuck runs silently burn the daily quota; detection quality decides cost per resolved bug.

nodes.label: Edit formats (diff vs whole-file)
nodes.summary: How the model expresses a change: search/replace blocks, unified diff, whole file. They fail differently.
nodes.whyItMatters: The edit contract decides how often a correct idea becomes a malformed or misapplied patch.

nodes.label: Gate feedback to the loop
nodes.summary: Lint, type, test and verifier results are fed back as observations so the agent can repair itself.
nodes.whyItMatters: Ground truth from the environment is what separates a loop that converges from one that guesses.

nodes.label: Context budget management
nodes.summary: Treat the window as a budget: decide what is kept, trimmed or dropped at each step.
nodes.whyItMatters: Quality degrades and quota burns as context grows; the budget policy is an ADR-level decision.

source.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents (Anthropic)

nodes.label: Compaction & summarization
nodes.summary: Replace old turns with a summary, or offload big outputs to files; a summary that does not shrink the view fails.
nodes.whyItMatters: Long runs need it, but it can break the prompt cache and lose the one fact that mattered.

source.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents (Anthropic)

nodes.label: Multimodal ticket context
nodes.summary: Attach the ticket screenshot only in image mode and only if bytes match the declared media type.
nodes.whyItMatters: Images cost tokens and quota; whether they raise success is an empirical question (ADR-005).

nodes.label: Prompt caching
nodes.summary: Reuse a stable prompt prefix across calls at a lower price and, on some hosts, without quota charge.
nodes.whyItMatters: Ordering a prompt for cache hits is the biggest cost lever, and compaction can destroy it.

nodes.label: Model routing
nodes.summary: Send each step to a cheap or strong model based on difficulty.
nodes.whyItMatters: Routing trades resolve rate against tokens and quota; it must beat a single strong model to stay.

nodes.label: Cost modelling ($-equivalent)
nodes.summary: Tokens times published list prices, per bug, summed over retries, judges and samples.
nodes.whyItMatters: Cost per resolved bug, not per call, is what decides whether an agent is viable.

nodes.label: Token accounting (fresh vs cached)
nodes.summary: Input, output and cached tokens are tracked separately and never summed into one number.
nodes.whyItMatters: Providers bill and rate-limit these differently; merging them hides the caching lever.

nodes.label: Provider rate limits
nodes.summary: RPM, RPD, TPM and TPD limits per model, read from headers where possible and published tables otherwise.
nodes.whyItMatters: Free-tier limits throttle evals by wall clock; measure them rather than trusting a marketing page.

nodes.label: Quota ledger
nodes.summary: A persisted ledger checks the cap before the HTTP call and hard-stops with QuotaExceeded.
nodes.whyItMatters: Stopping before the call keeps a partial result from looking like a model failure.

nodes.label: Per-tenant quota budgets
nodes.summary: Split a provider quota into per-tenant shares so one tenant cannot starve the rest.
nodes.whyItMatters: Multi-tenancy turns the ledger from a safety stop into a fairness and billing primitive.

source.title: Stripe: Scaling your API with rate limiters

nodes.label: Git worktrees
nodes.summary: Check out a clean tree per task or run, so patches never touch the main checkout.
nodes.whyItMatters: Cheap isolation for filesystem state; the same trick lets many agents work in parallel.

nodes.label: Container sandbox (Docker, no network)
nodes.summary: Run untrusted generated scripts in a container with --network none.
nodes.whyItMatters: The baseline sandbox tier: cheap and fast, but it shares the host kernel.

nodes.label: gVisor (user-space kernel)
nodes.summary: Intercepts syscalls in a user-space kernel so a container escape needs a gVisor bug, not a Linux one.
nodes.whyItMatters: A middle tier: stronger isolation than Docker with less cold-start cost than a microVM.

nodes.label: Firecracker microVMs
nodes.summary: Each sandbox is a KVM microVM with its own kernel and a minimal device model.
nodes.whyItMatters: The strongest tier; needs KVM and costs startup time, so it must be measured, not assumed.

nodes.label: Sandbox tier selection
nodes.summary: Choose Docker, gVisor or Firecracker by trust level, cold start and escape-test pass rate.
nodes.whyItMatters: The architect skill is matching isolation strength to the threat, with numbers behind the choice.

nodes.label: Idempotency & dedup keys
nodes.summary: Make repeating an operation safe, using a key so a retry does not open a second PR or send a second message.
nodes.whyItMatters: At-least-once delivery is the norm; idempotency is what makes retries safe.

nodes.label: Durable execution
nodes.summary: Persist each step result and explicit state so a crashed workflow resumes without redoing completed steps.
nodes.whyItMatters: Agent runs are long and failure-prone; durability turns a crash into a pause.

nodes.label: DBOS (Postgres-backed workflows)
nodes.summary: A library that stores workflow state in Postgres and recovers in-process, with no separate server.
nodes.whyItMatters: The $0-friendly choice: durability on a free Postgres, with recovery rules you must respect.

nodes.label: Temporal (decision only)
nodes.summary: Server-based durable execution with replayed deterministic workflow code.
nodes.whyItMatters: Knowing when Temporal beats DBOS is the point of the ADR, even though Argus will not run it.

nodes.label: Transactional outbox
nodes.summary: Write the state change and the outgoing message in one transaction; relay the message after.
nodes.whyItMatters: The standard fix for "updated the DB but failed to notify"; durable steps solve the same problem.

nodes.label: Webhooks as hints
nodes.summary: Treat a webhook as a nudge that something changed, not as the source of truth.
nodes.whyItMatters: Webhooks get dropped, duplicated and delayed; with a 10 s timeout and cold starts, you cannot rely on them.

source.title: GitHub: Best practices for using webhooks

nodes.label: Reconciliation polling
nodes.summary: A periodic loop compares the desired state in GitHub with local state and repairs differences.
nodes.whyItMatters: Level-triggered reconciliation self-heals after any missed event; this is how Kubernetes controllers work.

nodes.label: Human-in-the-loop wait
nodes.summary: Pause a durable workflow until a QA signal arrives by message or review comment.
nodes.whyItMatters: Real pipelines wait for people; the wait must survive restarts and time out.

nodes.label: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
nodes.summary: A client/server protocol exposing tools, resources and prompts to a model host.
nodes.whyItMatters: The de facto way agents reach external tools; interop gaps are a real project risk.

nodes.label: MCP version negotiation
nodes.summary: Client and server settle on a protocol version at initialize; the pinned server spoke 2025-11-25, not 2026-07-28.
nodes.whyItMatters: You need a spike and an ADR, not an assumption, before building on a spec revision.

nodes.label: Authoring an MCP server
nodes.summary: Expose locate() as an MCP tool with a typed schema.
nodes.whyItMatters: Building the server side shows which schema and error choices hurt agents.

nodes.label: Stateless protocols
nodes.summary: Each request carries what the server needs; no session state is held between calls.
nodes.whyItMatters: Statelessness is what lets servers scale and restart; spec 2026-07-28 moves MCP this way.

nodes.label: MRTR (multi-round-trip requests)
nodes.summary: A server returns input_required, the client answers with inputResponses, so asking a human stays stateless.
nodes.whyItMatters: The 2026-07-28 spec replaces long-lived sessions with this; it is the MCP route for the QA signal.

nodes.label: Trajectory recording (JSONL)
nodes.summary: One record per step with tokens, raw response and stop reason, plus run metadata (model, host, seed, prompt hash, commit).
nodes.whyItMatters: If a run is not recorded with its provenance, you can neither replay it nor trust a number from it.

nodes.label: Trajectory replay
nodes.summary: Re-run a stored trajectory from its recorded reply with no model call.
nodes.whyItMatters: Replay makes CI deterministic and free; but it proves the harness, not the model.

nodes.label: Distributed tracing
nodes.summary: A trace is a tree of timed spans; an agent run maps to a root span with a child per step and tool call.
nodes.whyItMatters: You cannot debug or cost an agent without seeing the call tree.

nodes.label: OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions
nodes.summary: Standard span and attribute names (gen_ai.*) for model calls, agents and tools; still marked development.
nodes.whyItMatters: A vendor-neutral vocabulary lets you swap trace backends without rewriting instrumentation.

nodes.label: Trace backends (Langfuse / Phoenix)
nodes.summary: Ingest OTLP spans and show prompts, tokens and cost per trace.
nodes.whyItMatters: Free tiers cap volume, so the backend choice is a risk-register item.

nodes.label: Attribute normalizer
nodes.summary: Map between attribute dialects (OTel GenAI, OpenInference, vendor) so any backend reads one shape.
nodes.whyItMatters: Semantic conventions are in flux; a normalizer isolates you from the churn.

nodes.label: Trajectory metrics
nodes.summary: Steps, tool-error rate, redundant-call rate, stuck rate and recover-after-gate-failure rate.
nodes.whyItMatters: Resolve rate says whether it worked; trajectory metrics say why and where it wastes effort.

nodes.label: SWE-bench & Multimodal
nodes.summary: Real GitHub issues paired with fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass tests; a multimodal variant adds screenshots.
nodes.whyItMatters: The industry yardstick for issue-resolving agents; know what it does and does not measure.

nodes.label: Golden-fix regression CI
nodes.summary: Apply each known-good patch and require its checks to pass, with no model calls.
nodes.whyItMatters: A deterministic gate that proves the benchmark itself is sound on every push.

nodes.label: Tri-state verdicts (pass / fail / infra)
nodes.summary: Scorer exits 0 for pass, 1 for check failure, 2 for infra or missing tree.
nodes.whyItMatters: Treating a crash as a failure corrupts your denominator; infra is its own outcome.

nodes.label: Mutation testing
nodes.summary: Inject small syntactic faults to see whether checks notice; here the mutants become the benchmark bugs.
nodes.whyItMatters: The classic technique for judging whether tests catch real changes, reused here to manufacture bugs.

nodes.label: Synthetic bug generation
nodes.summary: Deterministic JSX/CSS operators produce bugs at scale; the same seed yields the same task set.
nodes.whyItMatters: Hand-written bugs cannot reach statistical power; synthetic ones need validity rules to be trusted.

nodes.label: Mutant validity filter
nodes.summary: Keep a mutant only if checks fail on it and pass on the original, with a non-empty check list.
nodes.whyItMatters: It separates real check failures from build breaks and infra errors that would pollute the set.

nodes.label: Flaky-test quarantine
nodes.summary: Score each tree five times; if outcomes disagree or any is infra, move the task out of the set.
nodes.whyItMatters: Flaky tasks add noise that looks like model variance; quarantine before sampling.

source.title: Flaky Tests at Google and How We Mitigate Them

nodes.label: Wilson confidence interval
nodes.summary: A binomial interval that stays sensible at small n and at 0 or 100 percent.
nodes.whyItMatters: With 10 to 30 tasks, a point rate is nearly meaningless; differences inside the interval are no difference.

source.title: Binomial proportion confidence interval: Wilson score (Wikipedia)

nodes.label: Ablation design
nodes.summary: Change one factor on a fixed task set and compare; the text-only vs text-plus-image run is the first.
nodes.whyItMatters: Ablations are how you earn the right to keep a component.

nodes.label: Fixture replay testing
nodes.summary: Replace the model with recorded replies so the pipeline can be tested offline and repeatably.
nodes.whyItMatters: Great for harness regressions, but numbers from it must not be read as model quality.

nodes.label: CI regression gate
nodes.summary: Fail the build when resolve rate, tokens or latency worsen beyond thresholds backed by an interval.
nodes.whyItMatters: Without a gate, every prompt tweak can silently erode quality.

nodes.label: LLM-as-judge
nodes.summary: A model grades a fix against a written rubric; also check for order (position) bias by swapping candidates.
nodes.whyItMatters: Some properties have no deterministic check, but a judge is itself a measured instrument.

source.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena (arXiv 2306.05685)

nodes.label: Self-preference bias
nodes.summary: Models tend to rate outputs from their own family higher.
nodes.whyItMatters: It is why the intent judge comes from a different family than the fixer, and why that is ablated.

source.title: LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations (arXiv 2404.13076)

nodes.label: Inter-rater agreement (Krippendorff's alpha)
nodes.summary: Chance-corrected agreement between raters (human and judge); percent agreement is not alpha.
nodes.whyItMatters: Alpha is the number that says whether the judge is usable at all.

nodes.label: Judge calibration
nodes.summary: Label about 100 pairs by hand, then iterate the rubric until judge-human agreement clears a threshold.
nodes.whyItMatters: An uncalibrated judge gives confident noise; the plan defines what to do if the bar is unreachable.

source.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena (arXiv 2306.05685)

nodes.label: Best-of-k sampling
nodes.summary: Sample k candidate fixes and keep the one a verifier prefers; a form of test-time compute scaling.
nodes.whyItMatters: It raises resolve rate at k times the quota; the cost cap is part of the design.

nodes.label: Fail-before / pass-after validity
nodes.summary: A repro script counts only if it fails on the buggy tree and passes on the fixed one.
nodes.whyItMatters: A repro that passes on the bug (or fails on the fix) is noise; this rule is the oracle for the whole pipeline.

nodes.label: Computed-style assertions
nodes.summary: Assert a CSS property on an element via getComputedStyle after rendering.
nodes.whyItMatters: The cheapest deterministic UI check; many CSS bugs show up here without pixels.

nodes.label: Pixel diff
nodes.summary: Compare two screenshots pixel by pixel with a per-pixel colour threshold.
nodes.whyItMatters: Catches visual regressions that selectors miss, but is brittle without masks and AA handling.

nodes.label: Masks for dynamic regions
nodes.summary: Hide timestamps, avatars and animations before diffing, without reflowing the page.
nodes.whyItMatters: Unmasked dynamic content makes visual tests flaky and trains people to ignore them.

nodes.label: Anti-aliasing & thresholds
nodes.summary: Tune colour threshold, AA detection and allowed pixel count so a 4 px real shift still fails.
nodes.whyItMatters: Too loose hides real regressions; too strict flags font rendering noise.

nodes.label: Accessibility checks (axe)
nodes.summary: Run axe-core rules for WCAG violations such as contrast and missing labels on the rendered page.
nodes.whyItMatters: A fix can pass visually and still break accessibility; axe makes that a gate.

nodes.label: Verifier pipeline & gate ordering
nodes.summary: Run cheap gates (overflow, console, axe) first, short-circuit before the judge, publish as a check run.
nodes.whyItMatters: Ordering is a cost decision; the judge must not override a failed deterministic check.

nodes.label: DOM-to-source mapping (data-src)
nodes.summary: A Vite plugin stamps each JSX element with file:line:col so a DOM node maps to code at build time.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the shortcut that makes UI bugs cheap to locate; React 19 removed the old debug source field.

nodes.label: Source maps
nodes.summary: A file mapping generated code positions back to the original source.
nodes.whyItMatters: The classic alternative to data-src; knowing why Argus does not use it is part of ADR-006.

nodes.label: Repo map
nodes.summary: A ranked summary of files and symbols in a small token budget; LSP definitions/references are the precise alternative.
nodes.whyItMatters: Gives the agent structural orientation without reading whole files.

nodes.label: Embeddings retrieval (pgvector)
nodes.summary: Embed code chunks, store vectors in Postgres, retrieve by similarity; evaluate by top-1 file accuracy.
nodes.whyItMatters: Semantic search is the common default; the ablation tests whether it beats the repo map.

nodes.label: Prompt injection
nodes.summary: Untrusted text (issues, pages, tool output) steers the agent; never interpolate it into CI shell steps.
nodes.whyItMatters: Ticket text is attacker-controlled input to a system that can run code and push commits.

nodes.label: Threat modelling
nodes.summary: List assets, trust boundaries and attacker goals, then map each threat to a control.
nodes.whyItMatters: Sandbox tiers, token scopes and audit logs only make sense against a stated threat model.

nodes.label: OWASP agentic threats (ASI01-10)
nodes.summary: A catalogue of risks specific to agents: goal hijack, tool misuse, privilege abuse, memory poisoning.
nodes.whyItMatters: It gives a shared vocabulary and checklist for the P7 threat model.

source.title: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026

nodes.label: Least-privilege tokens
nodes.summary: Give the agent a short-lived, repo-scoped token with only the permissions the step needs.
nodes.whyItMatters: Handing the agent contents:write on a long-lived token is the most common avoidable blast radius.

source.title: GitHub: Generating an installation access token

nodes.label: Automated red-teaming (promptfoo)
nodes.summary: Run generated adversarial cases against the agent and grade deterministically.
nodes.whyItMatters: Defences you have not attacked are assumptions, not controls.

nodes.label: Skill trust & poisoned skills
nodes.summary: A distilled skill is executable influence; review it, scope it and test it against poisoning.
nodes.whyItMatters: A skill learned from trajectories is a persistence channel for bad instructions.

nodes.label: GitHub Apps
nodes.summary: An installable identity with per-repo permissions, webhooks and short-lived installation tokens.
nodes.whyItMatters: The correct integration model for a bot used across repos, replacing personal access tokens.

nodes.label: Tenancy via reusable workflows
nodes.summary: Tenants run a shared workflow in their own repo, so code and secrets stay on their side.
nodes.whyItMatters: It sidesteps hosting untrusted code for others, at the cost of per-tenant configuration.

nodes.label: Backporting
nodes.summary: Cherry-pick a merged fix onto release branches and open PRs, with a defined conflict policy.
nodes.whyItMatters: Real maintenance work is mostly this; conflict handling decides whether it is safe to automate.

nodes.label: Planner & subagent pattern
nodes.summary: A planner decomposes work and delegates to subagents with isolated contexts.
nodes.whyItMatters: It adds cost and failure modes; keep it only if it wins on both success and tokens.

source.title: How we built our multi-agent research system (Anthropic)

nodes.label: Agent skills (agentskills.io)
nodes.summary: A folder with SKILL.md that an agent loads on demand (progressive disclosure).
nodes.whyItMatters: Skills package procedural knowledge without paying for it in every prompt.

nodes.label: Skill distillation from trajectories
nodes.summary: Turn successful runs into reviewed skills, then test on held-out bugs.
nodes.whyItMatters: It is the lightweight path to learning from experience; the held-out split keeps it honest.

nodes.label: Backend lane (Sentry event to test)
nodes.summary: Turn a production error event into a failing pytest, then reuse the fix loop.
nodes.whyItMatters: It tests whether the loop, verifier and flow generalize beyond UI bugs.

nodes.label: Architecture decision records
nodes.summary: Short documents recording context, decision, alternatives and consequences.
nodes.whyItMatters: At architect level the reasoning outlives the code, and ADRs are how you show it.
